blocks.p: A maritime lien is a privileged claim against the vessel herself rather than against any person. It is not created by agreement and it is not registered: it attaches to the ship by operation of law at the moment the claim arises, and it does so without notice to anyone. Until it is enforced it is inchoate - a right in the ship that lies dormant; it is crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale. Its practical significance is its rank: a maritime lien takes priority over a registered mortgage, even one registered earlier and for a far larger sum.
That combination - secret, unregistered, automatic and senior - is what distinguishes it from an ordinary possessory lien, which depends on holding the goods and is lost when possession is given up.

blocks.h: 2. How the lien travels with the property

blocks.p: This is the defining characteristic, and the Convention states it in one sentence. Article 8: the maritime liens follow the vessel, notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag.

ul: The lien is attached to the res - the ship - and not to the owner, so selling the ship does not shed it.

It binds a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. A buyer may acquire a ship with unpaid crew wages or a salvage award still charged against her and have no means of discovering it from any register. This is why it is called a secret lien and why prudent buyers take indemnities and searches.
Reflagging and re-registration make no difference: the lien travels with the hull, not with the certificate.
It is defeated in only two ways - by a forced sale complying with article 12, which sweeps the ship clean of liens and encumbrances, or by lapse of time under article 9.

blocks.p: Under article 9 the article 4 liens are extinguished after one year unless, before then, the vessel has been arrested or seized and that arrest or seizure leads to a forced sale. Time runs from the claimant's discharge from the vessel for wage claims and from the moment the claim arises for the others, and it runs continuously, without suspension or interruption.

ul: An action in personam is brought against a person - the owner, charterer, manager or operator. The claimant must find that person, establish jurisdiction over them, and then enforce against whatever assets they have. If the defendant is a single-ship company with no other assets, a judgment in personam may be worth nothing.

An action in rem is brought against the ship herself, which is named as defendant. The court's jurisdiction is founded on the presence of the res within the jurisdiction, and the ship may be arrested.

blocks.p: The connection between the two limbs of this question is the point the examiner is looking for: the maritime lien is what gives the claimant a right in rem against the ship. Because the lien attaches to the vessel and follows her, the claimant can proceed against the vessel wherever she is found and whoever now owns her.

Arrest is not usually an end in itself. It is a coercive step: it either compels the provision of security - a P&I club letter of undertaking or a bank guarantee - so that the ship may trade on, or, if no security is forthcoming, it produces a fund through forced sale out of which the claims are paid. The two forms of action are not alternatives and may be pursued together.

blocks.h: 4. Which convention deals with maritime liens

blocks.p: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force from 5 September 2004. It is the successor to the earlier Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967 on the same subject, neither of which achieved wide acceptance. Its stated purpose is to improve the conditions for ship financing and the development of national merchant fleets - which explains its structure: it protects mortgagees by making mortgages recognisable and enforceable across States, and it does so by defining exhaustively the small class of claims that outrank them.
Article 4(1) secures five claims, against the owner, demise charterer, manager or operator, by a maritime lien on the vessel:

ul: (a) claims for wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the vessel's complement in respect of their employment on the vessel, including costs of repatriation and social insurance contributions payable on their behalf;
(b) claims in respect of loss of life or personal injury, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel;
(c) claims for reward for the salvage of the vessel;
(d) claims for port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues;
(e) claims based on tort arising out of physical loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss of or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects carried on the vessel.

blocks.p: Article 4(2) removes two categories from limbs (b) and (e): damage from the carriage of oil or other hazardous or noxious substances for which compensation is payable under regimes providing strict liability and compulsory insurance, and damage from the radioactive properties of nuclear fuel, products or waste. The reasoning is that those claimants already have a dedicated fund, and there is no need to give them a lien as well.

Note what is not a maritime lien: cargo claims, and the claims of necessaries men - bunker suppliers, repairers and agents. They may be maritime claims founding an action in rem, but they carry no lien under article 4.

blocks.h: 6. How the liens rank among themselves - article 5

ul: The article 4 liens take priority over registered mortgages, "hypotheques" and charges, and no other claim takes priority over either, subject to article 12(3) and (4).
They rank in the order listed in article 4 - so wages before personal injury, before salvage, before dues, before tort.

But salvage liens jump the queue: a lien securing a claim for salvage reward takes priority over all other maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed. The logic is obvious - the salvor preserved the very fund the others are claiming against.
Liens within each of (a), (b), (d) and (e) rank pari passu among themselves.
Salvage liens rank in the inverse order of time in which the claims accrued - the later salvage ranks first - each claim being deemed to accrue on the date the salvage operation terminated.

blocks.h: 7. The order of settlement after forced sale - article 12

blocks.p: A forced sale in a State Party sweeps the vessel clean: all registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges, except those assumed by the purchaser with the holders' consent, and all liens and other encumbrances of whatsoever nature, cease to attach to the vessel, provided the ship was within that State's jurisdiction and the sale complied with its law and with articles 11 and 12. The proceeds are then distributed in this order:

ul: 1. The costs and expenses of the arrest or seizure and of the subsequent sale, paid first out of the proceeds. These expressly include the costs of upkeep of the vessel and the crew, and the wages and other sums under article 4(1)(a) incurred from the time of the arrest or seizure.

2. Wreck-removal costs, where a State Party has so provided. Article 12(3) permits a State to provide that, where a stranded or sunken vessel has been removed by a public authority in the interest of safe navigation or protection of the marine environment, those removal costs are paid before all other claims secured by a maritime lien. This is optional, not automatic.
3. The article 4 maritime liens, in their article 5 order and subject to the salvage rules.

4. The right of retention of a shipbuilder or shiprepairer under article 7. Article 12(4) requires him to surrender possession to the purchaser, but entitles him to be satisfied out of the proceeds after the article 4 lienholders.
5. Registered mortgages, "hypotheques" and charges complying with article 1.
6. Other maritime liens granted under national law under article 6, which rank after both the article 4 liens and the registered mortgages.
7. The residue, if any, to the owner, and States Parties must ensure the proceeds are actually available and freely transferable.

blocks.p: The purchaser is then entitled to a certificate that the vessel is sold free of encumbrances, on production of which the registrar must delete the registered mortgages and charges and either register the vessel in the purchaser's name or issue a certificate of deregistration.

blocks.h: 8. The Indian statutory position, kept separate

blocks.p: In India the subject is governed domestically by the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (No. 22 of 2017, assented 9 August 2017), which consolidated admiralty jurisdiction and vested it in the High Courts. Its scheme closely follows the Convention, and the differences are worth knowing:

ul: Section 9(1) lists the same five maritime liens in the same order, with two widenings: limb (c) covers salvage including special compensation, and limb (d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel.

Section 9(2) reproduces the travelling rule - the lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag - and the one-year extinction, but with a proviso giving TWO years for wage claims under limb (a), running from the date the wage, repatriation cost or social insurance contribution fell due. That is more generous to seafarers than the Convention.

Section 10 sets the order of priority of maritime claims in an admiralty proceeding as: (a) claims where there is a maritime lien; (b) registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; (c) all other claims - with claims in a single category ranking equally, and salvage claims in inverse order of time.

blocks.p: (The stem asks about the convention, and the answer above is given at convention level. The Indian Act is set out separately because it is the law an Indian court would apply, and it should not be conflated with the Convention.)

The stem contains five separate demands in sixteen marks - define the lien, explain how it travels, explain in rem and in personam, name the convention, and give the order of settlement. That is roughly three marks each, so none of them deserves an essay and none may be skipped. The two that candidates most often lose are the last: they name the convention vaguely, or give a half-remembered priority list. The order of settlement is the single most concrete thing in the question and it is the easiest to prepare, so it should be written out as a numbered list, not narrated.

blocks.h: The idea that links the whole question

blocks.p: The lien and the action in rem are two halves of one mechanism. The maritime lien attaches to the ship rather than to a person; that is precisely what allows the claimant to sue the ship rather than a person. If you state that link explicitly - the lien is what gives the right in rem - the middle three demands of the question join up instead of reading as three unrelated definitions.

blocks.h: Why the lien is called secret, and why that matters commercially

blocks.p: There is no register of maritime liens. A buyer inspecting the ship's registry sees mortgages and charges but cannot see unpaid crew wages, an outstanding salvage award or a personal injury claim - and under article 8 all of those follow the vessel through a sale, a change of registry and a change of flag. So a purchaser can take delivery of a ship already encumbered by claims ranking ahead of the mortgage financing the purchase. This is why sale contracts carry indemnities and why a forced sale under article 12 is commercially valuable: it is the one transaction that delivers a genuinely clean ship, which is exactly why an arresting creditor's remedy has teeth.

blocks.h: The two salvage rules - state both

blocks.p: Salvage is the exception to almost every ranking rule in the Convention and both exceptions are examinable.

ul: Salvage jumps ahead of earlier liens. A salvage lien takes priority over all maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed. The salvor preserved the fund everyone else is claiming against, so he is paid first out of it.

Salvage liens rank in inverse order of time. Where there is more than one salvage, the later ranks ahead of the earlier - each claim accruing on the date its salvage operation terminated. Every other category ranks pari passu.

blocks.h: What is NOT a maritime lien

blocks.p: A quick way to show command of article 4 is to say what it leaves out. Cargo claims are not secured by a maritime lien - article 4(1)(e) expressly excludes loss of or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects. Nor are the claims of necessaries men - bunker suppliers, repairers, agents and chandlers. These may still be maritime claims supporting an action in rem and an arrest, but they carry no lien and therefore rank behind registered mortgages. The distinction between a maritime claim and a maritime lien is exactly what the priority list is about.

blocks.h: The Indian dimension - and the statement to avoid

blocks.p: The examiner asks about the convention, so answer at convention level. The Indian statute is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, and giving it separately is a strength: its section 9 reproduces the five liens and their order, and its section 10 gives the three-tier priority - liens, then registered mortgages, then all other claims.

Two genuine Indian divergences are worth knowing. Section 9(1)(c) covers salvage including special compensation, and section 9(1)(d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel. Most importantly, section 9(2) gives seafarers two years for wage claims where the Convention gives one - more generous than the Convention.

What to avoid: do not assert whether or not India is a party to the 1993 Convention. It is not necessary to answer any part of this question, and a confident statement either way is a risk for no reward. Say what the Convention provides, say what the Indian Act provides, and let the two stand side by side.

ul: Confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien. Every lien is a claim; very few claims are liens.
Saying a maritime lien is lost on sale of the ship. It is not - article 8 is the whole point of the question's second limb.
Treating in rem and in personam as alternatives. They may be pursued together.
Putting mortgages ahead of maritime liens. Article 5 puts the liens first, which is the commercially surprising and therefore examinable point.
Forgetting that arrest and sale costs and post-arrest crew wages are paid before everything, including the liens.
Omitting the salvage inverse-order rule, or applying inverse order to all categories rather than only to salvage.
Giving a mortgage a rank ahead of the shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention. Article 12(4) puts retention after the article 4 liens but the Convention leaves mortgages behind both.

blocks.p:
"You buy a ship with a clean registry search. Can you still be caught?" Yes. Maritime liens are unregistered and follow the vessel through a change of ownership, registration and flag. Only a forced sale under article 12, or the lapse of time under article 9, clears them.

"Crew wages or the bank - who is paid first?" Crew. Article 4(1)(a) is the first maritime lien and article 5(1) puts all article 4 liens ahead of registered mortgages. And the wages incurred after arrest are paid even before that, as part of the article 12(2) costs.

"Two salvage services, one in January and one in June. Who ranks first?" June - salvage liens rank in inverse order of time.

"Is a bunker supplier's claim a maritime lien under the Convention?" No. It may be a maritime claim founding an action in rem, but article 4 does not secure it, so it ranks behind registered mortgages.

ul: Define a maritime lien in one sentence. A privileged claim attaching to the vessel by operation of law, without registration or notice, which follows her through changes of ownership, registration and flag.
Which convention, adopted where and when? The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004.

List the five maritime liens in order. Wages; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; tort for physical loss or damage other than to cargo, containers and passengers' effects.
How long does a maritime lien last? One year under article 9, unless arrest or seizure leading to forced sale intervenes - and two years for wage claims under the Indian Act.
What is paid first out of a forced sale? The costs of arrest, seizure and sale, including upkeep of ship and crew and post-arrest wages.
Where do mortgages rank? After the article 4 maritime liens and after a shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention.
Which Indian statute governs? The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - section 9 for liens, section 10 for priority.

blocks.p: For the five liens at step 5, W-P-S-D-T: Wages, Personal injury, Salvage, Dues, Tort. For the settlement order at step 7, work outward from the court: COSTS first, LIENS next, then the YARD, then the BANK, then the REST, then the OWNER. For the two salvage rules, salvage jumps forward, and later salvage beats earlier.

questions.understand_first: Ordinary law says that if you are owed money you sue the person who owes it. Shipping cannot work that way: the debtor may be a single-ship company in a jurisdiction you will never reach, and the only asset is a ship that will sail tomorrow. So maritime law does something unusual - it lets a small class of claims attach to the SHIP itself, silently and automatically, and follow her wherever she goes and whoever buys her. That is a maritime lien, and the action in rem is simply the procedure for enforcing it: you sue the ship. Everything else in this question - the priority list, the arrest, the forced sale - is the machinery for turning a ship into money and then deciding who gets paid out of it, in what order.

retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a maritime lien is. 2 How it travels with the property. 3 In rem and in personam. 4 Which convention. 5 What article 4 secures. 6 How the liens rank among themselves. 7 The order of settlement after forced sale. 8 The Indian statutory position, separately.
retrieval_cards.why: Five demands in sixteen marks, so about three marks each. None deserves an essay and none may be skipped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a maritime lien.
retrieval_cards.answer: A privileged claim against the vessel herself, attaching to her by operation of law at the moment the claim arises, without agreement, registration or notice. It is inchoate until enforced, crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale, and it ranks ahead of registered mortgages.
retrieval_cards.why: Secret, unregistered, automatic and senior - those four words distinguish it from every ordinary lien.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a maritime lien travel with the property, and how is it ever lost?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 8 of the 1993 Convention: the maritime liens follow the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag - so they bind even a bona fide purchaser without notice. They are lost only by a forced sale complying with article 12, which sweeps the ship clean, or by lapse of time under article 9 - one year, unless arrest or seizure leading to a forced sale intervenes.
retrieval_cards.why: The travelling rule is the second demand of the stem and the Convention answers it in a single sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish an action in rem from an action in personam, and say how the lien connects them.
retrieval_cards.answer: In personam is against a person - the owner, charterer, manager or operator - and is worth only what that person's assets are worth. In rem is against the ship herself as defendant, founded on her presence within the jurisdiction and enforced by arrest. The maritime lien is what gives the claimant the right in rem, because it attaches to the vessel and follows her. The two may be pursued together.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the link turns three separate definitions into one mechanism, which is what the examiner is looking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the convention and list the five claims it secures by a maritime lien.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 - Geneva, 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004. Article 4: (a) crew wages, repatriation and social insurance; (b) loss of life or personal injury; (c) salvage reward; (d) port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; (e) tort for physical loss or damage, other than to cargo, containers and passengers' effects.
retrieval_cards.why: W-P-S-D-T. The order is the ranking order too, so learning the list once does two jobs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the order of settlement of claims after a forced sale under the 1993 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Costs and expenses of arrest or seizure and of the sale, including upkeep of vessel and crew and article 4(1)(a) wages incurred from the time of arrest. 2 Optionally, wreck-removal costs where the State has so provided under article 12(3). 3 The article 4 maritime liens in their article 5 order. 4 A shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention under article 12(4). 5 Registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges. 6 Other national maritime liens under article 6. 7 The residue to the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the most concrete thing in the question and the easiest to prepare. Write it as a numbered list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two salvage services, January and June. Which lien ranks first, and why does salvage rank oddly at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: June. Salvage liens rank in the inverse order of time in which the claims accrued, each accruing when its salvage operation terminated. Salvage also takes priority over all other maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed, because the salvor preserved the very fund the other claimants are claiming against.
retrieval_cards.why: Two separate salvage rules, and inverse order applies only to salvage - not to the other categories, which rank pari passu.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a bunker supplier's claim a maritime lien under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Bunker suppliers, repairers, agents and other necessaries men have maritime claims which may found an action in rem and support an arrest, but article 4 does not secure them by a maritime lien, so they rank behind registered mortgages. Cargo claims are excluded in terms by article 4(1)(e).
retrieval_cards.why: Every lien is a claim; very few claims are liens. Confusing the two is the commonest error in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Indian Admiralty Act 2017 differ from the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 9(1) lists the same five liens in the same order, but limb (c) covers salvage including special compensation and limb (d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel. Section 9(2) reproduces the travelling rule and the one-year extinction but adds a proviso giving two years for wage claims - more generous to seafarers than the Convention. Section 10 gives a three-tier priority: maritime liens, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims, with equal ranking within a category and salvage in inverse order of time.
retrieval_cards.why: It is an Indian examination, so the domestic statute earns marks - but keep it separate from the Convention rather than merging the two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Crew wages or the mortgagee bank - who is paid first out of a forced sale?
retrieval_cards.answer: The crew. Article 5(1) puts all article 4 maritime liens ahead of registered mortgages, and wages are the first lien in the article 4 list. Wages and upkeep incurred after the arrest rank even higher, as part of the article 12(2) costs paid first out of the proceeds.
retrieval_cards.why: It is commercially counter-intuitive that an unregistered claim beats a registered mortgage, which is exactly why it is examined.

blocks.h: 1. Where the energy to be recovered is

blocks.p: A screw propeller working behind a hull typically converts only about 65 to 72 per cent of delivered power into useful thrust. The losses are of three kinds: axial, in the sternward momentum of the race; rotational, in the swirl the blades impart to it; and frictional and vortex losses, principally the hub vortex shed from the boss. The rotational component alone is commonly of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw merchant ship.

The rudder is the only large body standing in that race. It is therefore both an opportunity - the swirl arrives at it already rotating, so a correctly oriented surface there sees an angle of attack for nothing - and a liability, because a plain rudder behind a bare boss adds drag and lets the hub vortex run on unchecked. The four devices below exploit the first and reduce the second.

A rudder thrust fin is a horizontal foil, usually fitted as a pair port and starboard, mounted on the rudder at or near the level of the propeller shaft, inside the slipstream. Because the race is rotating, the flow arrives at the fin with a tangential component: upward on one side of the shaft and downward on the other. Each fin is set at the angle that turns that oncoming flow into lift, and because the flow is inclined, the lift vector is tilted forward. Its horizontal component is thrust, generated with no additional power.

ul: The two fins are set at different angles, or in mirror image, because the swirl direction differs above and below the shaft.
Gains quoted in industry literature are typically of the order of 2 to 5 per cent in delivered power, and are strongly dependent on span, chord and angle of attack.
The angle is fixed at build. The device is optimised for one draught and speed and gives less, or in extreme off-design conditions nothing, elsewhere.
It is a source of added appendage drag when not loaded, and a candidate for cavitation erosion if it sits too close to the blade tips.

blocks.p: Here the recovery is built into the rudder itself rather than added to it. On a single-screw ship the propeller turns one way, so the race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other. A conventional symmetrical rudder, aligned with the centreline, therefore meets the flow at an angle of attack of the wrong sign over half its span, producing side force, drag and early cavitation.

An asymmetric rudder cures this by making the two halves different. In the developed form - the twisted leading edge rudder - the leading edge is twisted in opposite directions above and below the shaft line, so that each half is aligned with the swirl it actually meets.

ul: The rudder becomes a swirl-recovery surface: the side force on the two halves is turned into a net forward component.
It reduces drag and cavitation, and with it rudder erosion and propeller-excited vibration.
It is handed - built for one direction of rotation - so it is a design decision, not a universal retrofit.
Because it changes the rudder body rather than adding to it, it carries no added appendage and its benefit degrades more gracefully off design than a fixed fin.

blocks.p: The propeller boss sheds a strong hub vortex, and behind a bare boss the flow separates, leaving a low-pressure wake that pulls the ship astern. A rudder bulb is a streamlined body of revolution fitted to the rudder leading edge, coaxial with the shaft and sized and positioned so that it forms an almost continuous body with the propeller hub cap, closing the gap between them.

ul: It suppresses or displaces the hub vortex, removing a pure loss.
It restores pressure behind the boss by giving the flow a body to close around instead of separating, which is a genuine reduction in resistance rather than a recovery of energy.
The diameter and the axial gap govern the result; too large or too far aft and the bulb adds more drag than it saves.
It is most often fitted together with fins, the bulb conditioning the flow the fins work in, so the two are designed as one installation and their savings are not simply additive.

blocks.p: The vane wheel, patented by Otto Grim in 1966, is the most ambitious of the four and the only one that moves. It is a freely rotating bladed wheel mounted on the shaft line immediately aft of the propeller, of larger diameter than the propeller, with no mechanical connection to it or to the shaft. It runs at its own speed, typically around a third to a half of propeller revolutions, driven entirely by the water.
Its cleverness is that one blade does two jobs at different radii:

ol: The inner portion, standing inside the propeller race, works as a turbine. It extracts energy from the swirl and axial velocity of the slipstream, and that is what drives the wheel round.

The outer portion, standing outside the race in undisturbed water, works as a propeller. Driven by the torque the inner part has extracted, it produces additional thrust over a larger disc area and therefore at higher efficiency.

blocks.p: The wheel thus takes wasted energy from a small, fast, disturbed stream and returns it as thrust in a large, slow, clean one. Gains of the order of 5 to 10 per cent were claimed and some were demonstrated. In service the device proved difficult: the long, thin, unsupported blades of the outer portion are fatigue-loaded and blade loss and shedding occurred; performance falls away in a seaway and off design, when the wheel can windmill unhelpfully; and it adds a rotating component aft of the propeller with its own bearing and clearance problems. It is now of more importance as a principle - and as an examination question - than as a device in general service.

blocks.h: 6. Whether a claimed gain is real on this ship

blocks.p: All four claims are hull-specific. A device recovers only what the propeller behind that hull actually wastes, so the gain depends on the wake field, block coefficient, propeller loading, draught and service speed. Three consequences follow, and they are where the marks are at this level. First, a quoted percentage means nothing without the condition it was measured in, and model-scale results require a scale-effect correction before they can be believed at full scale. Second, devices interact: a bulb changes the flow the fins see, so savings must be assessed for the installation as a whole. Third, the real case is the operating profile - a ship that spends its life slow-steaming at part draught will not realise a gain optimised for design condition, and the payback calculation must be built on the actual profile, on class approval of the attachment and its structure, and on the effect on manoeuvring, which a rudder-mounted device necessarily touches.

The examiner has done the structuring for you. Four devices are named and each carries 4 marks, so the answer is four equal blocks and nothing else can be substituted for them. The single most common way to lose marks here is to write a good general essay on energy-saving devices - pre-swirl stators, ducts, propeller boss cap fins, air lubrication - none of which is asked for. Answer the four printed limbs.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks all four

blocks.p: Rotational loss. The propeller leaves the race spinning, and that spin is energy already paid for and thrown away. Two of these devices recover it - the fin and the twisted rudder turn swirl into forward force, and the vane wheel takes it mechanically. Two stop further waste - the bulb removes the hub vortex and the separation behind the boss. If you can say which of the two categories a device is in, you can reconstruct its explanation from first principles.

blocks.h: Keep recovery and drag reduction apart

ul: Recovery - thrust fins, asymmetric and twisted rudders, vane wheels. They convert energy already in the water into thrust.
Drag and vortex reduction - rudder bulbs. They do not recover anything; they stop a loss from happening.

The bulb is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy. The defensible statement is that it suppresses the vortex and restores pressure behind the boss. Say that and the point is safe either way.
Describing an asymmetric rudder as a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. The asymmetry is in the section and the twist about the shaft line, matching the opposite swirl above and below.
Saying the Grim vane wheel is geared to or driven by the shaft. It is entirely free-running; there is no mechanical connection, and that is the whole point.
Making the vane wheel the same diameter as the propeller. It is larger, and it must be, because the outer portion has to stand outside the race to act as a propeller.
Quoting a saving as a hard number. Every figure is conditional on the hull and the operating condition.
Adding the percentages of several devices together.
Ignoring manoeuvring. Anything bolted to a rudder changes the way she steers, and class will want to see the structure.

"Currently in use" in the stem. The Grim vane wheel is the odd one out - historically important, largely not in service. Say so rather than pretending it is common; an answer that quietly treats all four as current practice is weaker, not stronger.
Limb (d) is worth the same 4 marks as the others even though it is the least used. Do not short it.
The stem says the devices contribute to propulsion effectiveness, not to steering. Manoeuvring belongs in the closing judgement, not in place of the hydrodynamics.

questions.understand_first: A propeller does not convert all the power it is given into useful thrust. Some of what it leaves behind is axial - water thrown astern faster than it needs to be - and some is rotational: the race leaves the disc spinning, and that spin is wasted energy. Behind the propeller of a single-screw ship sits a large flat object in exactly that spinning race: the rudder. Every device in this question does one of two things with it - it either recovers some of the rotational energy and turns it into forward thrust, or it stops wasting more, by removing a vortex or a separation the rudder itself creates. Read the four limbs that way and they stop being four unrelated gadgets.

quick_revision.recall_15s: The idea. A propeller leaves the race spinning; rotational loss is of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power, and the rudder sits in it. (a) Thrust fins - horizontal foils on the rudder at shaft level, set to the swirl so their lift tilts forward; the horizontal component is thrust. Fixed angle, so optimised for one condition. (b) Asymmetric / twisted rudders - the rudder section itself twisted in opposite senses above and below the shaft to match the opposite swirl; recovers side force as forward force and cuts drag and cavitation. Handed to the direction of rotation. (c) Rudder bulbs - a streamlined body on the rudder leading edge, coaxial with the shaft, closing the gap to the hub cap; suppresses the hub vortex and restores pressure behind the boss. Reduces loss rather than recovering energy. (d) Grim vane wheel - Grim, 1966; free-running, larger than the propeller, no mechanical connection; inner portion a turbine inside the race, outer portion a propeller outside it. Blade fatigue and off-design behaviour limited it in service. Judgement. Gains are hull-specific and condition-specific, do not simply add, need a scale correction from model scale, and must be tested against the real operating profile.
critical_numbers: Rotational loss in the propeller race is of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power - the pool all these devices draw on
Rudder thrust fins: gains industry-quoted at about 2 to 5 per cent, dependent on span, chord and angle of attack
Grim vane wheel: patented 1966; larger diameter than the propeller; runs at roughly a third to a half of propeller revolutions; gains claimed at about 5 to 10 per cent
Every one of these figures is conditional on hull, draught and speed, and none should be quoted as a guaranteed saving
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None governs the devices themselves. MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index and the operational carbon intensity rating - is the commercial driver for fitting them, and was in force well before this sitting.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing a general essay on energy-saving devices instead of the four printed limbs. The second trap is describing an asymmetric rudder as one offset from the centreline; the asymmetry is in the section and the twist about the shaft line. The third is saying the Grim vane wheel is driven by or geared to the shaft - it is entirely free-running, and that is the point of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the rudder-efficiency question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the losses are - then the four printed limbs in order: (a) thrust fins, (b) asymmetric and twisted rudders, (c) rudder bulbs, (d) Grim vane wheels - then the management judgement on whether a claimed gain is real on this ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner prints 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. The four blocks must be equal, and the surrounding material has to be paid for out of the same 16 marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the rotational loss, and why does it matter here?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller leaves its race spinning as well as moving astern. That swirl is energy already paid for and thrown away - of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw ship. The rudder stands directly in it, which is why the rudder region is where these devices work.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single idea behind all four devices. Knowing it lets you reconstruct any of them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a rudder thrust fin produce thrust without power?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a horizontal foil on the rudder inside the propeller race. The race is rotating, so the flow meets the fin at an angle of attack without the fin being turned. The fin develops lift, and because the oncoming flow is inclined the lift vector tilts forward; its horizontal component is thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism is the mark. Describing the fin's shape without the inclined-lift argument earns very little.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What exactly is asymmetric about an asymmetric rudder?
retrieval_cards.answer: The section and the twist about the shaft line, not the position. The propeller race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other, so the leading edge is twisted in opposite senses above and below the shaft to align each half with the swirl it actually meets.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest error is to describe a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. That is a different thing entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a rudder bulb recover energy or reduce loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Properly, it reduces loss. It suppresses the hub vortex and gives the flow a body to close around instead of separating behind a bare boss, restoring pressure there. It is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy; the safe formulation is suppression and pressure recovery.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one device in the four that is not a recovery device, and saying so shows you understand the mechanism rather than the marketing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain how a Grim vane wheel works.
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a freely rotating wheel aft of and coaxial with the propeller, larger in diameter, with no mechanical connection to the shaft. Its inner portion stands inside the propeller race and acts as a turbine, extracting energy from the swirl and driving the wheel round; its outer portion stands outside the race in clean water and acts as a propeller, converting that energy into additional thrust over a larger disc.
retrieval_cards.why: One blade doing two jobs at two radii is the whole idea, and it is what distinguishes the vane wheel from every other device on the list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a vane wheel be larger in diameter than the propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because its outer portion has to stand outside the propeller race to work as a propeller in undisturbed water. If the wheel were the same diameter, the whole blade would sit in the slipstream and there would be no propeller portion to return the extracted energy as thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: A favourite oral follow-up, and it tests whether the turbine-plus-propeller split has actually been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A maker offers a 4 per cent saving from a rudder thrust fin. What do you ask before agreeing?
retrieval_cards.answer: In what condition was the 4 per cent measured - draught, speed, loading - and was it model scale or full scale, with what scale correction? How does it behave at our actual operating profile rather than at the design point? What else is already fitted, since devices interact and savings do not simply add? What does class require for the attachment and its structure, and what is the effect on manoeuvring?
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level mark. Anyone can recite the mechanism; the Class I candidate interrogates the claim.

blocks.h: 1. a) What a general average act is

blocks.p: The statement in the question is correct, and the features are not a matter of opinion: they are drawn from the definition itself. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules provides that there is a general average act 'when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure'.

Note first how the Rules apply. They are not law: they take effect by incorporation into the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty - and the Rule of Interpretation then makes them apply 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. In India the concept is also recognised in the Marine Insurance Act 1963.
Every phrase of Rule A is doing work, and each yields one essential feature:

ol: Extraordinary. The sacrifice or expenditure must be outside the ordinary performance of the contract of carriage. Fuel burned on a normal passage, or wear on machinery in ordinary service, is not extraordinary however costly.

Intentional and voluntary. The loss must be deliberately incurred. Cargo washed overboard by a sea is accidental and lies where it falls; cargo jettisoned by decision is a sacrifice. This is the single feature that most sharply separates general from particular average.
Reasonable. Reinforced by the Rule Paramount, which overrides everything else: 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.'
Peril. There must be real danger - not necessarily immediate, but genuine and substantial, and more than the ordinary risk of the sea.

Common safety and common adventure. The act must be for the benefit of the whole adventure, not one interest alone, and there must be more than one interest at risk. A ship in ballast with no cargo on board has no common adventure and can have no general average.
Preservation of property. The purpose must be to preserve the property from that peril. Success matters: there must be something saved to contribute.

blocks.h: 3. The lettered rules that qualify the definition

ul: Rule C - only losses which are the direct consequence of the general average act are allowed. It expressly excludes demurrage, loss of market, loss caused by delay and any indirect loss whatsoever, and excludes environmental damage and the consequences of escaping pollutants.

Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties, without prejudice to any remedies or defences in respect of that fault. So the adjustment proceeds first, and blame is fought separately.
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the party claiming, who must give notice in writing to the average adjuster and supply particulars, generally within twelve months.

blocks.h: 4. How the loss is shared, and what general average is not

blocks.p: Under Rule A.2 the sacrifice is borne by the different contributing interests - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably in proportion to their values at the termination of the adventure. The adjustment is prepared by an average adjuster, and security is taken before cargo is released, normally an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter.

Two distinctions complete the picture. General average is not particular average: particular average is accidental damage, falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. And general average is not insurance: it is a rule of contribution between the parties to the adventure, which predates marine insurance entirely, though the contribution is in practice recoverable under the policy.

blocks.h: 5. b) The refloating scenario - the rule that governs it

blocks.p: This situation is dealt with expressly, and by a rule written for exactly these facts. Rule VII, 'Damage to Machinery and Boilers', provides:

'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.'

blocks.h: 6. Applying it - when the damage is allowed, and when it is not

blocks.p: Yes, the burnt bearings can be allowed in general average - provided four things are shown.

ol: The ship was ashore. She was aground, so the first condition is met on the facts given.

She was in a position of peril. This must be established, not assumed. A vessel lying safely aground on soft mud in fine weather, in no danger and awaiting the tide, is not in peril; one working on a hard bottom, or exposed to weather, tide or the risk of breaking her back, is. This is the condition on which the claim will actually turn.

The machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety. Running the engine ahead and astern to shake her off is precisely that - a deliberate act directed at the safety of the whole adventure, not a routine manoeuvre.

The damage arose at the risk of such damage. The master must have accepted the risk of damaging the engine as the price of refloating. Working an engine hard, astern and ahead, against a grounded hull is known to overload the bearings, and it is that knowing acceptance that makes the loss a sacrifice rather than an accident.

blocks.p: The damage then satisfies Rule A as well: it is extraordinary (not ordinary service), intentional (the engine was deliberately worked in a way likely to damage it), reasonable if refloating was a sensible response, and directed at the common safety. It is also the direct consequence of the act, as Rule C requires. Under Rule D it makes no difference to the right of contribution that the grounding may have been somebody's fault.

The converse must be stated, because it is the trap. Rule VII closes with an absolute prohibition: where the ship is afloat, damage from working the propelling machinery is 'in no circumstances' allowed. So if she had already come off and the bearings burnt while manoeuvring clear, or if she were merely touching and not in peril, the same physical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo. The engine damage is identical; the legal answer is opposite; and what decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

Limb (a) is a 'discuss the statement' question, and the highest-scoring way to discuss it is to show that the essential features are not a list somebody invented but the clauses of the Rule A definition read one at a time. That converts a memory answer into an analytical one. Limb (b) is worth the same 8 marks and is decided by a single rule, so the answer must quote Rule VII, apply its four conditions to the facts, and then state the converse. An answer that says 'yes, it is a sacrifice' without naming the rule or testing peril has taken about half the marks available.

blocks.h: Why general average exists at all

blocks.p: It is far older than marine insurance and older than most maritime law - the principle is found in the Rhodian sea law and passed through Roman law into every modern maritime system. The problem it solves is one of incentives at the worst possible moment. If a master must jettison cargo to save the ship, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, then whoever owned that particular cargo would bear everything while the rest of the adventure was saved at his expense. Nobody would consent, and the master's decision would be contested at the moment when hesitation is most dangerous. Making the loss a shared loss removes the conflict: every interest knows that a sacrifice made for the common safety will be contributed to by all. Seen that way, general average is a rule about decision-making under peril, not really a rule about money.

blocks.h: Sacrifice versus accident - the line that decides everything

blocks.p: Almost every general average problem in an examination is a disguised question about whether the loss was chosen. Cargo swept overboard by a sea is an accident; cargo jettisoned is a sacrifice. An engine that fails on passage is an accident; an engine deliberately worked to destruction to refloat the ship is a sacrifice. Water damage from a leak is an accident; water damage from firefighting is a sacrifice. Rule VII is simply that same line drawn for one specific case - and the drafters drew it so firmly that they added an absolute prohibition for the afloat case, because otherwise every hard manoeuvre would generate a claim.

blocks.h: The four conditions of Rule VII, and which one is really in issue

blocks.p: Ashore; in a position of peril; an actual intention to float her for the common safety; at the risk of such damage. In practice the first and third are usually obvious on the facts and the fourth follows from them. The condition that is actually litigated is peril. A ship aground is not automatically in peril - the question is whether she was in real danger, having regard to the bottom, the weather, the tide, her condition and the exposure of the position. That is why a careful answer says the claim 'turns on establishing peril' rather than simply asserting it, and why the master's log, weather records and any surveyor's evidence matter so much afterwards.

blocks.h: Which version of the Rules applies

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules are contractual, not statutory. They apply because the bill of lading or charterparty says they do, which is why the Rule of Interpretation has to declare that they operate 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. The consequence is that the version in force between the parties may be the 1994, 2004 or 2016 text, depending on what the contract incorporates. On this question it does not matter: Rule VII is materially identical in all three. On other questions it can matter a great deal, so the habit of asking which version is incorporated is worth forming.

blocks.p: For limb (a), hold the six features in the order the definition gives them: EXTRAORDINARY - INTENTIONAL - REASONABLE - PERIL - COMMON - PRESERVING. Then three lettered rules as qualifiers: C direct only, D fault does not matter, E you must prove it. For limb (b), hold Rule VII as four conditions and one prohibition: ashore, in peril, intending to refloat, accepting the risk - but never when afloat.

blocks.p: This is among the most securely sourced questions on the paper. Every proposition in the answer is carried by the text of the York-Antwerp Rules 2016, read in the Comite Maritime International publication - the Rule of Interpretation, the Rule Paramount, Rules A to E and Rule VII, all quoted from the rule text itself. Rule VII was separately confirmed to be materially identical in the 1994 and 2004 versions, which is the point that matters given that the Rules apply by contractual incorporation. Nothing here is time-sensitive: the Rules were unchanged between this sitting and the build date, and general average is among the most stable doctrines in maritime law.

Two limitations are recorded honestly. questions.understand_first: General average is not insurance and not liability - it is a rule of contribution, and it is one of the oldest ideas in maritime law. The problem it solves is a problem of incentives at the worst moment: if the master must sacrifice one interest to save the whole adventure, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, the owner of that interest would be ruined for everyone else's benefit and would fight the decision. Making the loss shared removes the conflict. Everything in limb (a) follows from that purpose - the sacrifice must be deliberate (or there was no decision to protect), for the common safety (or there is nothing to share), and reasonable (or the decision does not deserve protection). And limb (b) is simply that same test applied to an engine: damage suffered because the master chose to risk the machinery to save the ship is a sacrifice; damage suffered in the ordinary course is not.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) Rule A: 'There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.' The essential features are the clauses of that sentence: extraordinary - outside the ordinary performance of the contract; intentional and voluntary - deliberately incurred, which is what separates a sacrifice from an accident; reasonable - reinforced by the Rule Paramount, 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred'; peril - real and substantial danger, more than the ordinary risk of the sea; common safety and a common adventure - for the whole adventure and not one interest, so with no cargo on board there is no general average; and preservation of property, so there must be something saved to contribute. Qualifiers: Rule C, only the direct consequence is allowed, and demurrage, loss of market, delay and any indirect loss are excluded; Rule D, the right to contribute is unaffected by the fault of a party, without prejudice to separate remedies; Rule E, the onus of proof is on the claimant, with notice to the average adjuster. Contribution is rateable on the values of ship, cargo and freight at the end of the adventure, adjusted by an average adjuster, with an average bond and average guarantee taken before cargo is released. It is not particular average, which is accidental and lies where it falls, and it is not insurance - it is contribution. The Rules apply by contractual incorporation, not as law. (b) Yes - under Rule VII. 'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.' Four conditions: she was ashore; she must be shown to have been in peril - the condition that is actually contested; the engine was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety, which working ahead and astern to shake her loose plainly is; and the damage arose at the risk of such damage, the master accepting that risk. The burnt bearings are then an extraordinary, intentional, reasonable sacrifice and the direct consequence of the act. But if she had been afloat, the identical damage would be particular average and the owner's own loss.

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) 'yes, it is a general average sacrifice' without naming Rule VII, without testing whether the ship was in a position of peril, and without stating the converse. Rule VII allows the claim only where the ship is ashore and in peril and the machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety at the risk of such damage - and it then prohibits absolutely, 'in any circumstances', any allowance for machinery damage caused by working the propelling machinery while the ship is afloat. A second trap in limb (a) is forgetting that there must be a common adventure: a ship in ballast with no cargo has no general average, because there is no other interest to contribute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the general average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a general average act is - the Rule A definition. 2 The essential features drawn from it. 3 The qualifying lettered rules C, D and E. 4 How the loss is shared, and what general average is not. 5 The refloating scenario and Rule VII. 6 Applying Rule VII to the facts, with the converse.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Rule A definition of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: The essential features are the clauses of this sentence. Quote it and the features write themselves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the essential difference between general average and particular average?
retrieval_cards.answer: General average loss is intentionally and reasonably incurred for the common safety of the whole adventure, and is shared rateably by all the contributing interests. Particular average is accidental damage which falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. The dividing line is whether the loss was chosen.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost every general average problem is a disguised question about whether the loss was deliberate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Quote Rule VII of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.
retrieval_cards.why: It decides limb (b) outright. The second half - the absolute prohibition when afloat - is the part candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A grounded vessel's main engine bearings burn out while working ahead and astern to refloat her. Is the damage general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, under Rule VII, provided four things are shown: that she was ashore; that she was in a position of peril; that the machinery was worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety; and that the damage arose at the risk of such damage. Working ahead and astern to shake her loose establishes the intention and the acceptance of risk. Peril is the condition that must actually be proved.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asks for justification, so the marks are in applying the four conditions rather than in the yes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would the answer change if the ship had already been afloat when the bearings burnt?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, completely. Rule VII provides that where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average. The identical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: Same physical damage, opposite legal answer. What decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The grounding was caused by the master's negligence. Does that defeat the general average claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule D provides that rights to contribution in general average shall not be affected though the event which gave rise to the sacrifice may have been due to the fault of one of the parties to the common maritime adventure, but without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against or to that party in respect of that fault. The adjustment proceeds; blame is dealt with separately.
retrieval_cards.why: It keeps the adjustment moving. Cargo interests can still sue the owner for the fault - they simply cannot use it to refuse to contribute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is in ballast with no cargo on board and you sacrifice equipment to save her. Is there general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule A requires the act to be for the common safety and for the purpose of preserving property involved in a common maritime adventure. With no cargo there is only one interest at risk, no common adventure and nothing to contribute, so the loss falls entirely on the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: The word common in the definition is a condition, not decoration, and this is the quickest way to test whether it has been understood.

blocks.h: 1. A) What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: STCW refuses to treat competence as something that time served automatically confers. It replaces experience with demonstrated competence, and then addresses the conditions - fitness, rest, teamwork and company responsibility - under which competence can actually be exercised. The instrument is the STCW Convention and Code, 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force from 1 January 2012.

ul: The Part A tables of competence specify, for every function and level, the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods for demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard, not an examiner's impression.
Part A is mandatory; Part B is guidance - a distinction worth stating explicitly.

The Manila amendments added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention. It is the explicit recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a team.
Regulation I/6 governs training and assessment, and regulation I/8 requires a quality standards system, so the training system itself is audited rather than assumed.
Regulation I/11 requires periodic revalidation, and chapter VI mandatory safety familiarisation and basic training before a seafarer is assigned duties.

blocks.h: 3. Fitness for duty - the physical human being

ul: Regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those with designated safety, security and pollution-prevention duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require that watch systems are arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The Manila-amended A-VIII/1 minimum rest is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

Authorised exceptions are tightly conditioned: weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours in any 7-day period, exceptions from the 77-hour norm may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
The Manila amendments also introduced alcohol limits for masters, officers and other seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards, and regulation VIII/2 with section A-VIII/2 governs watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

blocks.h: 4. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: Regulation I/14 makes the company responsible for ensuring that seafarers hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their duties and with the ship's arrangements, and that documentation is maintained - so the human element is not left as an individual's problem. Administrations operate quality standards systems and are subject to independent evaluation and reporting to IMO.

blocks.h: 5. B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The guidance is MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and in MLC 2006. The Guidelines are arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party:

ul: Module 1 - Fatigue: what it is and its causes, grouped as sleep and rest, the biological clock and circadian rhythm, health and stress, environmental factors such as noise, vibration and motion, sleep disorders and operational factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company: assessing, mitigating and managing fatigue risk in the safety management system, in manning decisions and in scheduling.

Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer: practical guidance for the master, officers and ratings on sleep quality, diet and the limits of countermeasures - notably that caffeine is not a substitute for sleep.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design: mitigation designed in - accommodation location, noise, vibration, lighting and habitability.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities: how regulators and inspectors should approach it.

blocks.h: 6. How the guidance and the rules fit together

blocks.p: The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are set by a prescriptive formula in STCW chapter VIII, and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested: managers must allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and - in the Guidelines' own words - rest means rest, not the substitution of a different form of work. The same theme runs through MLC 2006 Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7. A management-level engineer should therefore treat recorded compliance as the floor, and a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant as a warning rather than a reassurance.

Two printed limbs of 8 marks each, so split the answer evenly and head each limb clearly. Limb A rewards structure - competence tables, fitness for duty, company responsibility - and limb B rewards naming the actual circular. A candidate who writes generally about tiredness for the second limb without producing MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its module structure will lose most of eight marks, because 'the IMO guidance' is a specific document.

blocks.h: The organising idea for limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on three fronts, and saying so gives the limb a spine: can they do it (competence standards, assessed against published criteria), are they fit to do it now (fitness for duty - rest, medical, alcohol), and who is responsible for making that possible (regulation I/14, the company). The Manila amendments strengthened all three and added the fourth dimension the older Convention lacked - can they work as a team, through mandatory leadership and teamworking training.

blocks.h: The numbers you must get right

blocks.p: 10 hours in any 24, and 77 hours in any 7 days. Divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods. Exceptions may not go below 70 hours in any 7 days and may not run more than two consecutive weeks. Learn 10, 77, 2, 6, 14, 70 - and be careful, because 70 and 77 are both real figures doing different jobs: 77 is the norm, 70 is the floor under an authorised exception. Quoting 70 as the normal requirement is the classic error, and it is exactly the trap that a pre-2010 copy of the Code will lead you into.

This is worth a paragraph of its own because it caught this project. A freely available IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1 - STCW.6/Circ.1 - reproduces the 1995 Code: five paragraphs, 70 hours weekly, and no 14-hour interval provision at all. It looks entirely authoritative, it is on an official domain, and it is superseded. A candidate who revises from it will write 70 where 77 is required and will omit the 14-hour rule altogether. The lesson generalises: for any instrument that has been amended, the question to ask of a source is not 'is this official?' but 'which edition is this?'

blocks.p: The operative regime is STCW 1978 as amended, with the Manila amendments in force since 1 January 2012 and MSC.1/Circ.1598 since January 2019 - both long settled before this sitting, so nothing here needed re-anchoring from the later relatives of this question. A comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code is under way through the HTW Sub-Committee: HTW 10 met 5-9 February 2024, two months before this examination, and agreed the roadmap, the methodology and the list of areas to be reviewed, with adoption targeted for 2027. One of the acknowledged gaps is the treatment of hours of rest. Nothing had been adopted at the date of this paper. So write the Manila regime as the operative one and mention the review only as work in progress; do not present any reviewed text as though it were in force.

The sourcing limitation is real and is the reason for the wrong-edition warning above. MIW holds no licensed copy of the STCW Convention and Code, so the A-VIII/1 figures rest on a competent-authority restatement of the amended Code rather than on the Code text. Regulation VIII/1 is quoted at primary level because MSC.1/Circ.1598, which was read in full, reproduces it. This question is substantively identical to several other built objects in its family, which are deliberately kept identical: a correction to any one of them must be applied to all.

questions.understand_first: The phrase human element is not a polite word for human error. In STCW it means the whole set of conditions that decide whether a competent person actually performs competently on the day - whether the standard he was assessed against was published and objective, whether he has slept, whether he is medically fit, whether he can work as part of a team, and whether his company has made any of that possible. That is why limb A cannot be answered with rest hours alone: rest is one of four fronts. And it is why limb B is a separate document - the mandatory rule sets a floor for hours, while the Guidelines address the thing the floor cannot reach, which is whether the person is actually rested.

technical_ambiguities: 70 and 77 hours are both genuine figures in A-VIII/1 doing different jobs - 77 is the weekly norm, 70 the floor under an authorised exception. Presenting either as 'the' weekly requirement is wrong.

The fatigue Guidelines are recommendatory while the rest-hour requirements they discuss are mandatory. The answer must not blur the two, because the whole point of step 6 is that compliance with the mandatory formula does not discharge the duty to manage fatigue.
Fatigue is relevant to both limbs. It must be handled as fitness for duty in limb A and as the Guidelines in limb B, or the two limbs duplicate each other and the second earns nothing.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (A) Human element in STCW. The instrument is STCW 1978 as amended, above all by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force 1 January 2012. It replaces time served with demonstrated competence, then secures the conditions in which competence can be exercised. Competence: the Part A tables give, for each function and level, the competence, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency, the methods of demonstrating and the criteria for evaluating - and Part A is mandatory while Part B is guidance. Manila added mandatory leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level, bringing engine-room and bridge resource management into the Convention. reg I/6 training and assessment, I/8 quality standards, I/11 revalidation, chapter VI familiarisation before duties. Fitness for duty: reg VIII/1 requires Administrations, to prevent fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods per section A-VIII/1 - 10 hours in any 24 and 77 hours in any 7 days, in no more than two periods one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rests. Authorised exceptions may not fall below 70 hours weekly, may not run beyond two consecutive weeks, and allow no more than three daily periods. Manila also added alcohol limits; reg I/9 sets medical standards and reg VIII/2 watchkeeping arrangements. Responsibility: reg I/14 puts valid certification, familiarisation and documentation on the company; Administrations run quality standards subject to independent evaluation. (B) Fatigue guidance. MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory; the binding rest hours stay in STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006. Six modules: 1 Fatigue and its causes, defining sleep debt; 2 the Company; 3 the Seafarer; 4 Awareness and Training; 5 Ship Design; 6 the Administration and Port State Authorities. How they fit: hours of rest are a prescriptive formula, and compliance is not the same as being rested - allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and treat an always-exactly-compliant record as a warning.
critical_numbers: Manila amendments in force 1 January 2012
Minimum rest: 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period
Daily rest in no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours; interval between consecutive rest periods not more than 14 hours
Authorised exceptions: not below 70 hours in any 7-day period, not more than two consecutive weeks, daily rest then in no more than three periods

quick_revision.critical_regulation: STCW regulation VIII/1 with section A-VIII/1 for fitness for duty and hours of rest, and regulation I/14 for company responsibility; with MSC.1/Circ.1598 as the IMO guidance on fatigue.
quick_revision.major_trap: Quoting 70 hours as the normal weekly rest requirement. The norm is 77; 70 is the floor that applies only where an exception has been authorised. This error has a specific and dangerous source: a freely available IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1, STCW.6/Circ.1, reproduces the pre-Manila 1995 text - five paragraphs, 70 hours weekly and no 14-hour interval provision at all. It looks official because it is official; it is simply the wrong edition. The second trap is treating MSC.1/Circ.1598 as mandatory - it is recommendatory, and the binding requirements are in STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006. The third is answering limb B with general remarks about tiredness instead of naming the circular and its six modules.
